scenes.narration: Look up on a clear day. The sky is blue. But sunlight is white, so where does all that blue come from?
scenes.visual: A bright daytime sky, with the question popping up over it.

scenes.narration: White light is really every color mixed together. Each color is a wave, and blue waves are much shorter than red ones.
scenes.visual: A rainbow splitting out of white light, then short blue waves beside long red waves.

scenes.narration: In our atmosphere, that light runs into tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules, far smaller than the waves themselves.
scenes.visual: The Earth's atmosphere with tiny molecules floating in it.

scenes.narration: Those molecules scatter short waves far more than long ones. It's called Rayleigh scattering, and blue scatters about five times more than red.
scenes.visual: Light bouncing off molecules in every direction, with a big 5x stat.

scenes.narration: So blue light bounces all over the sky and reaches your eyes from every direction.
scenes.visual: Blue light arriving at a pair of eyes from all around.

scenes.narration: Violet scatters even more, so why not a purple sky? The sun sends less violet, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.
scenes.visual: A purple sky that fades back to blue.

scenes.narration: At sunset, light crosses so much air that the blue scatters away, leaving reds and oranges. Same physics, different sky.
scenes.visual: A warm orange sunset, ending on the takeaway line.
